module2.vision: We want to become a world-class, sustainable waterworks by 2035. We want to achieve highly potable, 24/7 water supply. We see a more effective waterworks company capable of providing reliable and safe/clean water to every household in Tagbilaran City.
module2.mission: Our mission is to provide our customers in 10/15 barangays in Tagbilaran City with safe and reliable water. Our employees are capable and highly trained. We strive to treat every customer fairly and respectfully and address their needs quickly and effectively.

objectives.title: Improve billed volume
objectives.relevant: Lack of water supply (SWOT weakness); production fell from 9.7 MLD (2023) to 7.7 MLD (H1 2025). TCWS serves 10 of 15 barangays and about 27% of the city population; approx. 33% of households in its 10 barangays. Billed volume flat at 1.7–1.9 M m3/yr since 2020; connections fell from 6,461 (2024) to 6,314 (2025).
objectives.specific: Increase billed volume by expanding to unserved areas (Cabawan, Booy, Cogon, Dampas, Bool), assessing and upgrading existing pump stations, and replacing old and inaccurate meters.
objectives.kpi_formula: Sum of billed volume over the year; count of active service connections
objectives.time_bound: Coverage expansion project: Years 1–4 (2026–2029), PhP 22.9 M. New main lines for bulk water: Years 2–4, PhP 119.4 M.

objectives.title: Reduce NRW to 20%
objectives.relevant: NRW of 39.9% (2024) is about double the 20% or below standard; 46% in 2023 and 48–54% in monthly checks (2021–2022). Old galvanized iron pipes in Tiptip, Manga and Ubujan.
objectives.specific: Reduce physical and commercial losses by identifying illegal connections, establishing 6 DMAs covering all service areas, and replacing old pipes in Manga, Ubujan and Taloto.
objectives.baseline: 39.9% (3,049,028 m3 produced; 1,833,134 m3 billed). H1 2025: 31.3% (provisional, production partly estimated).
objectives.time_bound: 26% by 2030; 20% by 2035. Pipe replacement project: Years 1–4 (2026–2029), PhP 113.1 M.

objectives.title: Improve collection efficiency
objectives.relevant: Negative bottom line (SWOT weakness); lack of training in billing and collection; collection efficiency is not currently calculated.
objectives.specific: Improve collection through enforcement of disconnections (review service contracts) and staggered accounts receivable payment schedules and policies.
objectives.baseline: Not available (collections known: PhP 22.9 M in 2024; billings not recorded)

objectives.title: Manage cost recovery
objectives.relevant: Low tariff is the number one weakness. Tariff unchanged since September 2016 (PhP 62 minimum for 10 m3; block rates PhP 7–23/m3). About PhP 12.5 collected per m3 (2024) vs. PhP 17.68/m3 needed to recover OPEX. Negative bottom line.
objectives.specific: Recover costs by setting up an LEE with a ring-fenced waterworks account and improving OPEX efficiency (energy efficiency, monitoring of fuel and electricity unit costs).
objectives.target: 1.00 or below. Proposed tariff: PhP 214.03 for the first 10 m3 (Years 1–5) and PhP 267.52 (Years 6–10).
objectives.time_bound: Years 1–5 and 6–10 of the tariff plan

objectives.title: Manage / improve after-sales service
objectives.relevant: Tariff increases must be balanced with better service. Billing process to be digitalized.
objectives.specific: Formalize customer service standards: no-water complaints (simple 24–48 h; complex 5–7 working days); mainline leaks within 24 h; illegal tapping investigated within 2 days; daily bulletins during interruptions; new applications inspected within 24–48 h and approved within 7 working days.
objectives.kpi_formula: Cases resolved within standard time / Total cases received

areas.key_indicators: Revised vision, mission and values (Nov 2025); 5 strategic objectives; CAPEX PhP 255.4 M in the plan vs PhP 579.2 M in the financial model (2026–2029)
findings: New vision: world-class, sustainable waterworks with 24/7 potable supply by 2035.
Five objectives defined: billed volume, NRW, collection, cost recovery, after-sales service.
Three priority projects: pipe replacement (PhP 113.1 M), coverage expansion (PhP 22.9 M), new main lines for bulk water (PhP 119.4 M).
Plan is preliminary; objectives lack owners, annual targets and timelines.
The plan and the financial model are not aligned (CAPEX, OPEX scenario, volume base of the tariff).
areas.message: Clear direction is in place; objectives now need owners, annual targets and deadlines to become an executable plan.

areas.key_indicators: Tariff unchanged since Sept 2016; PhP 12.5 collected per m3 vs PhP 17.68/m3 cost-recovery tariff (2024); collection efficiency not measured
findings: Connections grew from 5,612 (2020) to 6,461 (2024) but fell to 6,314 (2025); 99% residential; average consumption 23.6 m3/connection/month.
Billed volume flat at 1.7–1.9 M m3/yr since 2020.
Block tariff unchanged since Sept 2016 (PhP 62 minimum for 10 m3; PhP 7–23/m3; commercial PhP 23/m3; 15% late penalty).
Collections rose from PhP 18.7 M (2020) to PhP 23.1 M (2023) and PhP 22.9 M (2024); billings are not recorded, so collection efficiency cannot be measured.
Collections per m3 (PhP 12.5) look high for the 2016 tariff and need to be reconciled.
Meters are purchased by customers and are not always replaced when required.
areas.message: A 2016 tariff, flat volumes and no billing records make the revenue base the critical constraint.

areas.key_indicators: NRW 39.9% (Level 1); NRW 21.6 l/conn/h (Level 3); continuity 23.9 h/day, 93% of customers 24/7 (Level 4); availability 168 l/cap/day (Level 4)
findings: NRW 46% (2023) and 40% (2024); 31% in H1 2025 is provisional because several production readings are repeated month to month.
Production is declining: 9.7 MLD (2023), 8.4 MLD (2024), 7.7 MLD (H1 2025).
26 pumping units (160.5 HP) on deep wells, all with production meters and chlorinators.
Old galvanized iron pipes in Tiptip, Manga and Ubujan; no DMAs yet; no preventive maintenance.
Supply gap of 11.7 MLD against projected city demand.
areas.message: Continuity is good, but about 40% of produced water is lost while production declines; cutting NRW is the cheapest source of new supply.

areas.key_indicators: EBITDA margin -12.8% (Level 1); operating cost coverage 88.7% (Level 3); operating ratio 1.13 (2023)
findings: Revenue PhP 23.1 M vs OPEX PhP 26.1 M (2023): operating loss of about PhP 3.0 M.
Negative bottom line acknowledged by the utility.
Operates as a Local Economic Enterprise (LEE), not funded by the general fund; accounts not yet ring-fenced.
Proposed tariff (PhP 214.03 for the first 10 m3) is based on a volume that includes private providers' water; on TCWS bulk volume alone the required average tariff would be about PhP 50/m3.
areas.message: Revenues do not cover operating costs; tariff reform and ring-fenced LEE accounts are required for cost recovery.

areas.key_indicators: 9 regular staff + 15 job-order (24 total, 6 female); 1.39 regular staff per 1,000 connections (Level 5); 3.7 including job-order
findings: Lean staffing ratio, well below the 1:250 industry average.
Heavy reliance on job-order staff (63% of workforce).
Multi-tasking of personnel and unclear organizational structure.
Training needs in technical, finance, billing and collection, management and water safety planning.
No data on turnover or HR costs.
areas.message: The team is lean and committed but stretched; formalize the structure and invest in technical, finance and billing skills.

findings: 10% of samples fail national drinking water standards (PNSDW).
Chlorinators installed in all pump stations.
Water quality monitoring and compliance identified as a weakness.
areas.message: Disinfection is in place, but a 10% sample failure rate requires a water safety plan and stronger monitoring.

areas.key_indicators: Water coverage 27% of city population (Level 1); approx. 33% of households in the 10 served barangays
findings: Serves 10 of 15 barangays; other providers (BWUI, Richli) supply most of the city.
Expansion to Cabawan, Booy, Cogon, Dampas and Bool planned; 11,908 households to benefit by 2039.
TCWS does not provide sanitation services.
areas.message: Coverage is low even inside its own service area; expansion depends on new supply and investment.

areas.key_indicators: 10 of 22 performance indicators can be calculated; 19 data inconsistencies found across sources
findings: No data on billings, metering, customer satisfaction, complaints, turnover or HR costs; no 2024 OPEX.
Connection breakdown by barangay is repeated unchanged across 2022–2025 records.
Production readings repeated month to month in 2025; some units at zero in late 2024.
Business plan, financial model and utility records report different connections, NRW, CAPEX and revenue labels.
areas.message: Data quality is a binding constraint; reconcile one set of baseline figures before setting targets.

messages.text: TCWS provides reliable water to its customers but is not financially sustainable: the tariff has not changed since 2016, about 40% of produced water is lost, and revenues fall short of operating costs.
Average performance level across the 10 measurable indicators: 2.9 of 5 (between Basic and Good).
Raise revenue: adjust the tariff toward cost recovery, linked to visible service improvements.
Reduce NRW from 40% to 20% through DMAs, pipe replacement and control of illegal connections.
Fix the data: record billings, verify production meters, and align the plan with the financial model.
Ring-fence the waterworks account and assign owners and deadlines to each objective.
Build staff capacity in technical operations, finance, billing and water safety.

strengths.text: Already a Local Economic Enterprise (LEE), not funded by the general fund
Chlorinators installed in all pumping stations
Responsive team, especially in emergency services
Reliable supply of 22–24 hours per day
Lean staffing ratio (1.4 regular staff per 1,000 connections)

weaknesses.text: Old galvanized iron pipes (parts of Tiptip, Manga, Ubujan)
Need for training of technical and finance personnel
Lack of training for billing and collection, management and water safety plans
Water quality monitoring and compliance (10% failure in sampling)
High NRW (40% in 2024) and no district metered areas
Billings not recorded, so collection efficiency cannot be measured
Declining production (9.7 MLD in 2023 to 7.7 MLD in H1 2025)
Inconsistent data across records, plan and financial model

opportunities.text: Availability of bulk water supply in a few years
NGOs and private organizations that help improve water services (e.g., USAID, Maynilad)
Support from other local water utilities (collaboration with BWUI)
Proposed tariff is financially viable and affordable (2% of low-income household income)
Expansion to 5 unserved barangays; 11,908 households to benefit by 2039
City commitment to digitalize billing and keep TCWS public

threats.text: Natural hazards such as typhoons and earthquakes (standby gensets in selected pump stations)
Deep well sources of private institutions, establishments and businesses
Competition from other water providers in the city (BWUI, Richli)
Rising electricity costs (power is the largest projected OPEX item)
Customer resistance to tariff increases without visible service improvement

module3.review_notes: Validated annual NRW is 39.9% in 2024; the 31.3% H1 2025 estimate is provisional. Financial indicators use matched 2023 collections and OPEX as a cash-based proxy, not accrual revenue. Reconcile tariff volume denominators, OPEX versions and CAPEX totals before approval. Coverage uses 6,393 domestic connections and the 106,120 census population; older barangay breakdowns are not current.

module8.executive_summary: TCWS serves 6,461 connections at December 2024, falling to 6,314 in December 2025. Annual NRW improved from 46.3% in 2023 to 39.9% in 2024. The 2016 block tariff remains in place. Collections were PhP 22.89 million in 2024; billings are unavailable. Priorities are loss reduction, billing controls, staff capacity and financially sustainable expansion. The financial model proposes PhP 579.2 million CAPEX in 2026–2029 and PhP 114.1 million in 2035. These projections are preliminary: tariff denominators, OPEX assumptions and the difference from the PhP 255.4 million plan must be reconciled before investment or tariff decisions.

data_review.previous: BP: 6,084 connections "as of June/August 2025" (6,017 res / 34 com / 33 inst).
data_review.supporting: Utility records: 6,461 (Dec 2024) and 6,314 (Dec 2025). 6,017/34/33 equals the per-barangay breakdown list, which is repeated unchanged across 2022–2025 sheets.
data_review.action: Use 6,461 (2024) and 6,314 (2025). The per-barangay breakdown is not updated by the utility; do not use it.

data_review.previous: BP uses 1,897,357 m3 (2023) and 5.26 MLD (H1 2025); 2024 not reported.

data_review.supporting: Annual records: 46.3% (2023), 39.9% (2024); monthly spot checks 48–54% (Dec 2021, Dec 2022). Financial model: 51% (2022), 60% (2023), 44% (2024). The 31% in H1 2025 relies on production data with repeated (likely estimated) monthly readings.
data_review.action: Report NRW 2024 = 39.9% as baseline; treat 31% as provisional until production metering is verified.

data_review.supporting: Production fell from 9.69 MLD (2023) to 8.35 MLD (2024) and 7.66 MLD (H1 2025). Several units report zero in Sep–Dec 2024.
data_review.action: Confirm whether the decline is real (source depletion, pump failures) or a recording gap.

data_review.previous: BP: "Annual water sales 2024: PhP 22,887,685.65; Jan–Jun 2025: PhP 12,036,951.99".
data_review.supporting: Both figures are collections, not sales/billings; the 2025 figure covers Jan–Jul. Questionnaire shows 22,882,685.67 (typo).
data_review.action: Label as collections. Billings are still missing, so collection efficiency cannot be calculated.

data_review.previous: BP: "TCWS is charging PhP 6.20/m3"; Table 5 shows average tariff 13.76.
data_review.supporting: PhP 6.20 is only the minimum charge (PhP 62 for 10 m3). The block tariff (Sept 2016) goes from 7 to 23 PhP/m3; commercial 23 PhP/m3. 13.76 is the 2023 cost-recovery tariff, not the actual average.
data_review.action: Describe the tariff as the Sept 2016 block tariff; average collected 12.49 PhP/m3 (2024).

data_review.supporting: Collections/billed volume = 12.49 PhP/m3 (2024), but a typical residential bill (23 m3/month) under the 2016 tariff is about PhP 6.8/m3.
data_review.action: Check whether collections include arrears, penalties, connection fees or other income, or whether billed volume is under-recorded.

data_review.supporting: 2023 collections PhP 23,144,634.58 → operating ratio (OPEX/revenue) = 1.13; matches the financial model formula (Operating expenses / Operating revenue).
Financial model: PhP 579.2 M (2026–2029) + PhP 114.1 M (2035); includes meter replacement (PhP 166.8 M), fleet (PhP 27 M), DMAs, booster stations and contingencies.
data_review.action: Align the CAPEX figure in the plan with the model, or explain the difference.

data_review.previous: BP proposed tariff PhP 214.03 per first 10 m3.
data_review.supporting: The model divides the revenue requirement (PhP 334.5 M in 2030) by 15.25 M m3, which includes 8.56 M m3 from private providers (PWSP). On bulk water volume only (6.69 M m3), the required average tariff would be about PhP 50/m3, not PhP 21.9/m3.
data_review.action: Review the volume base of the tariff calculation.

data_review.previous: BP Table 15 uses power cost PhP 87.8 M (2030).
data_review.supporting: Model has two OPEX versions: PhP 13.13/m3 (OPEX sheet) vs PhP 10.3/m3 ("realistic" sheet). Chemical cost is zero in the OPEX sheet although PhP 0.5/m3 is assumed. A 10% service fee is added without explanation.
data_review.action: Select one OPEX scenario and fix the chemical cost link.

data_review.previous: BP KPI: "1 regular staff: 100 connections" and "1:250 industry average".
data_review.supporting: Model label "Staff (1:1000)" but applies 1 staff per 250 connections (42 staff in 2030 vs 24 today).

Model assumes 100% coverage of the whole city from 2025 (27,402 connections) while the tariff uses 10,493 connections in 2030; historical WSC in the model (5,867 in 2023; 5,873 in 2024) and billed volume (1,418,803 m3 in 2023) differ from utility records.
data_review.action: Update the demand sheet with utility records.

data_review.supporting: Production records and station profile list 26 pumping units (160.5 HP).
